claim: Serotonin (5-HT) acts as both a neurotransmitter and a hormone that regulates blood vessel constriction and intestinal motility.
source: 5-HT acts as both a neurotransmitter and a hormone that regulates blood vessel constriction and intestinal motility (Berger et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Berger et al., 2009, which provides external evidence for this assertion.

claim: 5-HT is a master regulator of circuits, physiology and behavioral functions including the sleep/wake cycle, sexual interest, locomotion, thermoregulation, hunger, mood, and pain.
source: Thus, 5-HT is a master regulator of circuits, physiology and behavioral functions including the sleep/wake cycle, sexual interest, locomotion, thermoregulation, hunger, mood, and pain (Berger et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Berger et al., 2009.

claim: 5-HT is cleared from synapses and taken into presynaptic neurons by the serotonin transporter (SERT), thus terminating serotonergic signaling.
source: 5-HT is cleared from synapses and taken into presynaptic neurons by the serotonin transporter (SERT), thus terminating serotonergic signaling (Gether et al., 2006; Kristensen et al., 2011; Rudnick et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gether et al., 2006; Kristensen et al., 2011; Rudnick et al., 2014.

claim: SERT belongs to a family of neurotransmitter sodium symporters (NSSs) which also includes the dopamine (DAT) and norepinephrine transporters (NET).
source: SERT resides in the plasma membrane of neurons and belongs to a family of neurotransmitter sodium symporters (NSSs) which also includes the dopamine (DAT) and norepinephrine transporters (NET) (Gether et al., 2006; Kristensen et al., 2011; Rudnick et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gether et al., 2006; Kristensen et al., 2011; Rudnick et al., 2014.

claim: NSSs are twelve transmembrane spanning secondary active transporters which utilize sodium and chloride gradients to energize the transport of neurotransmitter across the membrane.
source: NSSs are twelve transmembrane spanning secondary active transporters which utilize sodium and chloride gradients to energize the transport of neurotransmitter across the membrane (Rudnick et al., 2014; Navratna and Gouaux, 2019; Yamashita et al., 2005; Figure 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rudnick et al., 2014; Navratna and Gouaux, 2019; Yamashita et al., 2005, and is illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are a class of drugs which inhibit SERT and are used to treat major depression and anxiety disorders.
source: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are a class of drugs which inhibit SERT and are used to treat major depression and anxiety disorders (Cipriani et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cipriani et al., 2018.

claim: SSRIs are competitive inhibitors that bind with high-affinity and specificity to a central substrate-binding site in SERT, preventing 5-HT binding and arresting SERT in an outward-open conformation.
source: SSRIs are competitive inhibitors that bind with high-affinity and specificity to a central substrate-binding site in SERT, preventing 5-HT binding and arresting SERT in an outward-open conformation (Gether et al., 2006; Kristensen et al., 2011; Coleman et al., 2016a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gether et al., 2006; Kristensen et al., 2011; Coleman et al., 2016a.

claim: The central site in NSSs is composed of three subsites: A, B, and C.
source: The central site in NSSs is composed of three subsites: A, B, and C (Wang et al., 2013; Figure 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2013 and is illustrated in Figure 1b.

claim: In all NSS-ligand structures, the amine group of ligands resides in subsite A and interacts with a conserved Asp residue (Asp98 in SERT).
source: In all NSS-ligand structures, the amine group of ligands resides in subsite A and interacts with a conserved Asp residue (Asp98 in SERT).
evidence: The claim is based on structural knowledge from NSS-ligand structures.

claim: Paroxetine exhibits the highest known binding affinity for the central site of SERT (70.2 ± 0.6 pM) compared to any other currently prescribed antidepressants.
source: Paroxetine is an SSRI which exhibits the highest known binding affinity for the central site of SERT (70.2 ± 0.6 pM) compared to any other currently prescribed antidepressants (Cool et al., 1990).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cool et al., 1990.

claim: Paroxetine is frequently associated with serious side effects including infertility, birth defects, cognitive impairment, sexual dysfunction, weight gain, suicidality, and cardiovascular issues.
source: Despite its high affinity, paroxetine is frequently associated with serious side effects including infertility, birth defects, cognitive impairment, sexual dysfunction, weight gain, suicidality, and cardiovascular issues (Nevels et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nevels et al., 2016.

claim: X-ray structures of the SERT-paroxetine complex revealed that the piperidine ring binds to subsite A while the benzodioxol and fluorophenyl groups occupy subsite B and C in the central site, respectively (ABC pose).
source: X-ray structures of the SERT-paroxetine complex revealed that the piperidine ring binds to subsite A while the benzodioxol and fluorophenyl groups occupy subsite B and C in the central site, respectively (Coleman and Gouaux, 2018; Coleman et al., 2016a) (ABC pose, Figure 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Coleman and Gouaux, 2018; Coleman et al., 2016a and is illustrated in Figure 1b.

claim: Recent mutagenesis, molecular dynamics, and binding studies with paroxetine analogues suggest that paroxetine might occupy either ABC pose or an ACB pose where the benzodioxol and fluorophenyl groups occupy subsite C and B of the central site respectively.
source: However, recent mutagenesis, molecular dynamics, and binding studies with paroxetine analogues suggest that paroxetine might either occupy ABC pose as observed in the crystal structure, or an ACB pose where the benzodioxol and fluorophenyl groups occupy subsite C and B of the central site respectively (Abramyan et al., 2019; Slack et al., 2019; Figure 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Abramyan et al., 2019; Slack et al., 2019 and is illustrated in Figure 1c.

claim: The ts2-active variant contains two thermostabilizing mutations (Ile291Ala, Thr439Ser) and has kinetics of 5-HT transport (Km: 4.5 ± 0.6 μM, Vmax: 21 ± 5 pmol min−1) that are in a similar range as wild-type SERT (Km: 1.9 ± 0.3 μM, Vmax: 23 ± 1 pmol min−1).
source: The ts2-active variant contains two thermostabilizing mutations (Ile291Ala, Thr439Ser) which allows for purification of the apo transporter for binding studies and has kinetics of 5-HT transport (Km: 4.5 ± 0.6 μM, Vmax: 21 ± 5 pmol min−1) that are in a similar range as wild-type SERT (Km: 1.9 ± 0.3 μM, Vmax: 23 ± 1 pmol min−1) (Coleman et al., 2016a; Green et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Coleman et al., 2016a; Green et al., 2015.

claim: The ts2-inactive variant (Tyr110Ala, Ile291Ala) is unable to transport 5-HT but can be crystallized due to the stabilizing Tyr110Ala mutation and binds SSRIs with high-affinity.
source: The ts2-inactive variant (Tyr110Ala, Ile291Ala) (Coleman and Gouaux, 2018), by contrast, is unable to transport 5-HT but can be crystallized due to the stabilizing Tyr110Ala mutation (Green et al., 2015) and binds SSRIs with high-affinity.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Coleman and Gouaux, 2018; Green et al., 2015.

claim: The ΔN72/ΔC13 SERT variant used for cryo-EM is otherwise wild-type SERT which has been truncated at the N- and C-termini and yet retains transport and ligand-binding activities.
source: The ΔN72/ΔC13 SERT variant used for cryo-EM is otherwise wild-type SERT which has been truncated at the N- and C-termini (Table 1) and yet retains transport and ligand-binding activities (Coleman et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Coleman et al., 2019.

claim: Upon substituting the 4-fluoro group with 4-bromo or 4-iodo groups, the potency of inhibition of 5-HT transport in wild-type SERT decreased significantly from 4 ± 1 nM for paroxetine to 40 ± 20 nM for Br-paroxetine and 180 ± 70 nM for I-paroxetine.
source: We assayed the ability of the Br- and I-paroxetine derivatives to inhibit 5-HT transport in HEK293 cells expressing wild-type SERT, observing that upon substituting the 4-fluoro group with 4-bromo or 4-iodo groups, the potency of inhibition of 5-HT transport in wild-type SERT decreased significantly from 4 ± 1 for paroxetine to 40 ± 20 for Br-paroxetine and 180 ± 70 nM for I-paroxetine (Figure 3a, Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3a and Table 2.

claim: The ts2-inactive (Tyr110Ala, Ile291Ala) variant exhibited a Ki of 0.17 ± 0.02 nM for paroxetine, 0.94 ± 0.01 nM for Br-paroxetine, and 2.3 ± 0.1 nM for I-paroxetine.
source: For example, the ts2-inactive (Tyr110Ala, Ile291Ala) variant employed in the previous (Coleman and Gouaux, 2018) and present x-ray studies exhibited a Ki of 0.17 ± 0.02 nM for paroxetine, 0.94 ± 0.01 nM for Br-paroxetine, and a further decrease in affinity to I-paroxetine (2.3 ± 0.1 nM).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from binding assays.

claim: The ts2-active SERT variant binds with similar affinity to paroxetine and Br-paroxetine, and shows a 4–5 fold decrease in affinity to I-paroxetine.
source: The ts2-active SERT variant binds with similar affinity to paroxetine and Br-paroxetine, and shows a 4–5 fold decrease in affinity to I-paroxetine (Figure 3b, Table 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3b and Table 3.

claim: The affinity of paroxetine to ts2-active SERT decreased by three-fold when Asn177 is substituted with small non-polar or polar residues such as valine and threonine, while only a 2-fold change in Ki was observed for glutamine (Asn177Gln).
source: We observed that the affinity of paroxetine to ts2-active SERT decreased by three-fold when Asn177 is substituted with small non-polar or polar residues such as valine and threonine, while only a 2-fold change in Ki was observed for glutamine (Asn177Gln) (Figure 3c).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3c.

claim: In the case of Br-paroxetine, the Asn177 variants (Ki between 4 and 5 nM) display up to a 10–13 fold decrease in Ki when compared with ts2-active SERT (0.4 ± 0.2 nM).
source: In the case of Br-paroxetine, the Asn177 variants (Ki between 4 and 5 nM) display up to a 10–13 fold decrease in Ki when compared with ts2-active SERT (0.4 ± 0.2 nM) (Figure 3d, Table 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3d and Table 3.

claim: The Asn177 variants show 2–4 fold decrease in affinity to I-paroxetine, with ts2-active SERT exhibiting a Ki of 1.7 ± 0.3 nM and the mutants a Ki of 4–7 nM.
source: The Asn177 variants show 2–4 fold decrease in affinity to I-paroxetine, with ts2-active SERT exhibiting a Ki of 1.7 ± 0.3 nM and the mutants a Ki of 4–7 nM.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from binding assays.

claim: The structures of ΔN72/ΔC13 and ts2-inactive SERT bound to paroxetine analogues were determined using single-particle cryo-EM and x-ray crystallography, respectively.
source: To define the binding poses of paroxetine and its analogues to SERT, we solved the structures of the ΔN72/ΔC13 and the ts2-inactive SERT variants complexed with Br- and I-paroxetine using single particle cryo-EM and X-ray crystallography (Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data obtained from cryo-EM and X-ray crystallography, as shown in Figure 4 and its supplements.

claim: The ~ 3.3 Å resolution map of the ΔN72/ΔC13 SERT-8B6 paroxetine complex allowed location of a density feature for the inhibitor at the central site.
source: The ~ 3.3 Å resolution map of the ΔN72/ΔC13 SERT-8B6 paroxetine complex allowed us to locate a density feature for the inhibitor at the central site (Figure 4a).
evidence: The claim is supported by cryo-EM data presented in Figure 4a.

claim: The resolution of the Br- and I-paroxetine complexes was comparatively lower at ~ 4.1 Å and ~ 3.8 Å, respectively.
source: The resolution of the Br- and I-paroxetine complexes was comparatively lower at ~ 4.1 Å and ~ 3.8 Å, respectively (Table 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by cryo-EM data presented in Table 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Br- and I-paroxetine could be modeled into the density at the central site with a correlation coefficient (CC) of 0.75 and 0.77, respectively.
source: Nevertheless, these ligands could also be modeled into the density at the central site with a correlation coefficient (CC) of 0.75 and 0.77, respectively (Figure 4b–e).
evidence: The claim is supported by modeling data presented in Figure 4b–e.

claim: In the ACB pose, paroxetine could be positioned with a CC of 0.70 compared with 0.84 for the ABC pose suggesting that while ABC pose is clearly preferred under the conditions tested, the possibility of an ACB pose cannot be excluded.
source: We observed that in the ACB pose, paroxetine could be positioned with a CC of 0.70 compared with 0.84 for the ABC pose suggesting that while ABC pose is clearly preferred under the conditions we tested, the possibility of an ACB pose cannot be excluded (Figure 4—figure supplement 5a,b).
evidence: The claim is supported by modeling data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 5a,b.

claim: Anomalous difference maps calculated from the ts2-inactive paroxetine structure showed clear densities for Br- and I- atoms of the paroxetine derivatives in subsite C.
source: Anomalous difference maps calculated from the previously determined ts2-inactive paroxetine structure (PDB ID: 6AWN) after refinement, showed clear densities for Br- and I- atoms of the paroxetine derivatives in subsite C (Figure 4f,g).
evidence: The claim is supported by X-ray crystallography data presented in Figure 4f,g.

claim: No detectable anomalous peaks were observed in either subsite B or in the allosteric site and there were no other peaks in any other location above 2.5σ, suggesting that under these conditions, Br-paroxetine and I-paroxetine do not bind substantially in the ACB orientation or to the allosteric site.
source: No detectable anomalous peaks were observed in either subsite B or in the allosteric site and there were no other peaks in any other location above 2.5σ, suggesting that under these conditions, Br-paroxetine and I-paroxetine do not bind substantially in the ACB orientation or to the allosteric site.
evidence: The claim is based on the absence of anomalous peaks in X-ray data, leading to an inference about binding orientation.

claim: Overall comparison of the transporter revealed only minor variation between structures solved by cryo-EM and X-ray methods, with a Cα root-mean-square-deviation (RMSD) of 0.68 Å.
source: Overall comparison of the transporter revealed only minor variation between structures solved by each method, with a Cα root-mean-square-deviation (RMSD) of 0.68 Å.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural comparison data.

claim: The most significant differences between the cryo-EM and the X-ray structures were found at the extracellular and intracellular sites of TM12 and also in EL2, while the core of the transporter (TM1-10) was largely unchanged.
source: The most significant differences between the cryo-EM and the X-ray structures were found at the extracellular and intracellular sites of TM12 and also in EL2, while the core of the transporter (TM1-10) was largely unchanged (Figure 5a).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural comparison data presented in Figure 5a.

claim: The best fit to the cryo-EM density revealed only minor differences in the side-chains of Asp98, Tyr176, and Phe335 when compared to the x-ray structure (all atom RMSD: 0.91 Å).
source: We also compared central site residues involved in paroxetine binding, finding that the best fit to the cryo-EM density revealed only minor differences in the side-chains of Asp98, Tyr176, and Phe335 when compared to the x-ray structure (all atom RMSD: 0.91 Å) (Figure 5b).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural comparison data presented in Figure 5b.

claim: In the ABC pose, the amine of the piperidine ring of paroxetine binds with Asp98 (3.5 Å) and also makes a cation-π interaction with Tyr95 of subsite A.
source: In the ABC pose, the amine of the piperidine ring of paroxetine binds with Asp98 (3.5 Å) and also makes a cation-π interaction with Tyr95 of subsite A (Figure 4a).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data presented in Figure 4a.

claim: The benzodioxol group of paroxetine occupies a position in subsite B which is similar to the binding of catechol derivative groups of sertraline and 3,4-dichlorophenethylamine in SERT and dDAT structures, respectively.
source: The benzodioxol group of paroxetine, a catechol-like entity, occupies a position in subsite B which is similar to the binding of catechol derivative groups of sertraline and 3,4-dichlorophenethylamine in SERT (Coleman and Gouaux, 2018) and dDAT (Wang et al., 2015a) structures, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Coleman and Gouaux, 2018 and Wang et al., 2015a.

claim: In subsite B, the ring of Tyr176 makes an aromatic interaction with the benzodioxol while the hydrogen-bonding network in subsite B formed by Asn177, Thr439, backbone carbonyl oxygens, and amides are likely responsible for stabilization of the dioxol.
source: In subsite B, the ring of Tyr176 makes an aromatic interaction with the benzodioxol while the hydrogen-bonding network in subsite B formed by Asn177, Thr439, backbone carbonyl oxygens, and amides are likely responsible for stabilization of the dioxol.
evidence: The claim is based on structural observations and inference about hydrogen bonding interactions.

claim: The side-chain of Ile172 inserts between the benzodioxol and fluorophenyl, while the rings of Phe341 and Phe335 stack on either side of the fluorophenyl, 'sandwiching' it within subsite C.
source: The side-chain of Ile172 inserts between the benzodioxol and fluorophenyl, while the rings of Phe341 and Phe335 stack on either side of the fluorophenyl, 'sandwiching' it within subsite C.
evidence: The claim is based on structural observations.

claim: The halogen group of paroxetine and its analogues reside adjacent to the side-chain of Thr497 (4.0 Å), which may act to stabilize these groups through hydrogen bonding.
source: The halogen group of paroxetine and its analogues reside adjacent to the side-chain of Thr497 (4.0 Å), which may act to stabilize these groups through hydrogen bonding (Figure 4a).
evidence: The claim is based on structural observations and speculation about hydrogen bonding.

claim: The larger atomic radius, the longer length of the carbon-halogen bond, and the difference in electronegativity of bromine and iodine relative to fluorine would explain why the fluorine analogue binds with greater affinity than Br-paroxetine and I-paroxetine.
source: The larger atomic radius, the longer length of the carbon-halogen bond, and the difference in electronegativity of bromine (radius: 1.85 Å, bond-length: 1.92 Å, electronegativity: 2.96) and iodine (radius: 1.98 Å, bond-length: 2.14 Å, electronegativity: 2.66) relative to fluorine (radius: 1.47 Å, bond-length: 1.35 Å, electronegativity: 3.98) would explain why the fluorine analogue binds with greater affinity than Br-paroxetine and I-paroxetine.
evidence: The claim is based on chemical knowledge and inference from structural and binding data.

claim: Asn177 participates in a hydrogen-bond network with the hydroxyl group of noribogaine and with the dioxol of paroxetine.
source: Asn177 participates in a hydrogen-bond network with the hydroxyl group of noribogaine and with the dioxol of paroxetine.
evidence: The claim is based on structural observations.

claim: All the mutants tested at Asn177 resulted in a loss of binding affinity to paroxetine and its analogues.
source: All the mutants that we tested at Asn177 resulted in a loss of binding affinity to paroxetine and its analogues.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from binding assays.

claim: The Ala169Asp mutation in subsite B also reduced paroxetine inhibition and binding.
source: Furthermore, the Ala169Asp mutation in subsite B (Slack et al., 2019; Figure 1b,c) also reduced paroxetine inhibition and binding, likely also disrupting these interactions.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Slack et al., 2019.

claim: Using a combination of chemical biology, cryo-EM, and X-ray crystallography, the SSRI paroxetine preferably occupies the ABC pose at the central site under the conditions studied.
source: Using a combination of chemical biology, cryo-EM, and X-ray crystallography we observed that under the conditions that we studied, the SSRI paroxetine preferably occupies the ABC pose at the central site, where it is involved in numerous interactions.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence including cryo-EM, X-ray crystallography, and binding assays.

claim: The data presented in the manuscript does not completely exclude the possibility of an ACB pose at the central site.
source: However, the data presented in the manuscript does not completely exclude the possibility of an ACB pose at the central site.
evidence: The claim is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the data.

claim: C–H functionalization enabled installation of the appropriate aryl group on the pre-existing piperidine ring, providing an attractive and short route to vary this functionality with inherent control of enantiomeric excess.
source: Here, C–H functionalization enabled installation of the appropriate aryl group on the pre-existing piperidine ring (Antermite et al., 2018), providing an attractive and short route to vary this functionality with inherent control of enantiomeric excess.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Antermite et al., 2018.

claim: Pd-catalyzed C–H functionalization was achieved in moderate yields using 4-bromoiodobenzene or 1,4-diiodobenzene in excess to prevent bis-functionalization, with palladium acetate, K2CO3 and pivalic acid.
source: Adapting our reported method (Antermite et al., 2018), Pd-catalyzed C–H functionalization was achieved in moderate yields using 4-bromoiodobenzene or 1,4-diiodobenzene in excess to prevent bis-functionalization, with palladium acetate, K2CO3 and pivalic acid (Figure 2c).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Antermite et al., 2018 and experimental data presented in Figure 2c.

claim: The cis-arylated derivatives (+)−6a and (+)−6b were obtained with > 98% ee and complete C(4) selectivity.
source: The cis-arylated derivatives (+)−6a and (+)−6b were obtained with > 98% ee and complete C(4) selectivity.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the synthesis.

claim: Subsequent treatment with 1,8-diazabicyclo(5.4.0)undec-7-ene (DBU) gave complete C(3)-epimerization affording (+)−7a and (+)−7b with the desired trans-stereochemistry in 94% and 91% yields.
source: Subsequent treatment with 1,8-diazabicyclo(5.4.0)undec-7-ene (DBU) gave complete C(3)-epimerization affording (+)−7a and (+)−7b with the desired trans-stereochemistry in 94% and 91% yields.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the synthesis.

claim: The aminoquinoline group was removed through telescoped amide activation and reduction with LiAlH4 at 20°C to give enantiopure hydroxymethyl intermediates (–)−8a and (–)−8b in 77% and 75% yield.
source: The aminoquinoline group was removed through telescoped amide activation and reduction with LiAlH4 at 20°C to give enantiopure hydroxymethyl intermediates (–)−8a and (–)−8b in 77% and 75% yield.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the synthesis.

claim: Mesylation and nucleophilic substitution with sesamol formed ether derivatives (–)−9a and (–)−9b, which were deprotected to give Br- and I-paroxetine 2 and 3.
source: Mesylation and nucleophilic substitution with sesamol formed ether derivatives (–)−9a and (–)−9b, which were deprotected to give Br- and I-paroxetine 2 and 3.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the synthesis.

claim: An overall yield of 12% over 8 steps from commercial material was obtained in both cases for Br- and I-paroxetine synthesis.
source: An overall yield of 12% over 8 steps from commercial material was obtained in both cases.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the synthesis.

claim: The TM densities in all three reconstructions were well-defined and contiguous allowing for clear positioning of the main chain in an outward-open conformation.
source: The TM densities in all three reconstructions were well-defined and contiguous allowing for clear positioning of the main chain in an outward-open conformation (Figure 4—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by cryo-EM data presented in Figure 4—figure supplements 3 and 4.

claim: Large aromatic side-chains were well-resolved for all three complexes, suggesting that the aromatic moieties of paroxetine and its analogues could be identified and positioned in the cryo-EM maps.
source: Large aromatic side-chains were well-resolved for all three complexes, also suggesting that the aromatic moieties of paroxetine and its analogues could be identified and positioned in our cryo-EM maps.
evidence: The claim is based on cryo-EM data and inference about the ability to identify aromatic groups.

claim: The particle distribution and orientations of SERT-Fab complexes in presence of Br- and I-paroxetine were similar to paroxetine, allowing for uniform comparison between the maps.
source: In addition, the particle distribution and orientations of SERT-Fab complexes in presence of Br- and I-paroxetine were similar to paroxetine, allowing for uniform comparison between the maps.
evidence: The claim is based on cryo-EM data analysis.

claim: In the cryo-EM maps, the maltose headgroup of a DDM molecule could be visualized in the allosteric site with the detergent tail inserted between TMs 10, 11, and 12.
source: In the cryo-EM maps, the maltose headgroup of a DDM molecule could also be visualized in the allosteric site with the detergent tail inserted between TMs 10, 11, and 12.
evidence: The claim is based on cryo-EM data.

claim: In the X-ray maps only the head group of the octyl-maltoside detergent could be modeled due to the weak density of the hydrocarbon chain.
source: In contrast, in the X-ray maps only the head group of the octyl-maltoside detergent could be modeled due to the weak density of the hydrocarbon chain.
evidence: The claim is based on X-ray crystallography data.

claim: The Fo(paroxetine)-Fo(Br-paroxetine) map revealed a difference peak in subsite C near the halogenated groups while no significant peaks were detected in subsite B.
source: The Fo(paroxetine)-Fo(Br-paroxetine) map also revealed a difference peak in subsite C near the halogenated groups while no significant peaks were detected in subsite B (Figure 4—figure supplement 6a).
evidence: The claim is supported by X-ray crystallography data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 6a.

claim: The Fo(paroxetine)-Fo(I-paroxetine) map also contained a difference peak which overlapped with the position of the halogen.
source: Similarly, the Fo(paroxetine)-Fo(I-paroxetine) map also contained a difference peak which overlapped with the position of the halogen (Figure 4—figure supplement 6b)
evidence: The claim is supported by X-ray crystallography data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 6b.

claim: The Fo(Br-paroxetine)-Fo(I-paroxetine) difference map did not contain any interpretable features, likely due to the low resolution of both datasets.
source: while the Fo(Br-paroxetine)-Fo(I-paroxetine) difference map did not contain any interpretable features, likely due to the low resolution of both datasets (Figure 4—figure supplement 6c).
evidence: The claim is based on X-ray crystallography data and inference about the lack of interpretable features.

claim: These changes between cryo-EM and X-ray structures can largely be explained on the basis of a crystal packing interface formed by TM12 and a highly flexible EL2 that is bound to the 8B6 Fab.
source: These changes can largely be explained on the basis of a crystal packing interface formed by TM12 and a highly flexible EL2 that is bound to the 8B6 Fab.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from structural comparison.

claim: The most significant differences between the SERT 15B8 Fab/8B6 scFv paroxetine complex and the SERT 8B6 Fab paroxetine complex occurred in the extracellular domain and involved localized regions of EL2 and EL4 that interact with the antibody.
source: Here we found that the most significant differences occurred in the extracellular domain and involved localized regions of EL2 and EL4 that interact with the antibody (Figure 5c).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural comparison data presented in Figure 5c.

claim: The transporter core was largely unchanged between the SERT 15B8 Fab/8B6 scFv paroxetine complex and the SERT 8B6 Fab paroxetine complex, with the only other significant differences being found in EL6, TM12, and IL4.
source: The transporter core was largely unchanged, with the only other significant differences being found in EL6, TM12, and IL4.
evidence: The claim is based on structural comparison data.

claim: Paroxetine is thought to interact with the allosteric site of SERT, albeit with low-affinity.
source: Paroxetine is also thought to interact with the allosteric site of SERT, albeit with low-affinity (Plenge and Mellerup, 1985).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Plenge and Mellerup, 1985.

claim: The authors have been unable to visualize paroxetine binding at the allosteric site using structural methods.
source: We have, however, been unable to visualize paroxetine binding at the allosteric site using structural methods.
evidence: The claim is based on the absence of structural evidence.

claim: The X-ray maps resolve a density feature at the allosteric site which resembles a molecule of detergent.
source: Our x-ray maps, by contrast, resolve a density feature at the allosteric site which instead resembles a molecule of detergent (Coleman et al., 2016a).
evidence: The claim is supported by X-ray crystallography data and a citation to Coleman et al., 2016a.

claim: During the preparation of this work, the synthesis of Br-paroxetine was reported using an asymmetric conjugate addition and its binding to SERT has been extensively studied.
source: Nevertheless, during the preparation of this work, the synthesis of Br-paroxetine was reported using an asymmetric conjugate addition and its binding to SERT has been extensively studied (Slack et al., 2019; Brandau et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Slack et al., 2019; Brandau et al., 2006.

claim: Computational docking experiments using wild-type SERT predicted that the position of benzodioxol and fluorophenyl groups of paroxetine are 'flipped', with paroxetine occupying an ACB pose.
source: However, computational docking experiments using wild-type SERT predicted that the position of benzodioxol and fluorophenyl groups of paroxetine are 'flipped', with paroxetine occupying an ACB pose (Davis et al., 2016; Figure 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Davis et al., 2016 and is illustrated in Figure 1c.

claim: Subsequent studies involving wild-type and mutant SERT variants, that include modeling, mutagenesis, and Br-paroxetine docking experiments suggested that paroxetine could bind in both ABC and ACB poses.
